channel_name: No Priors · Elad Gil & Sarah Guo
video_title: Building an Autonomous Enterprise for Real-World Services with Netic Founder Melisa Tokmak
gist: Netic founder/CEO Melissa Tokmak (ex-Scale AI director of engineering) explains how her two-year-old company inserts AI agents between billion-dollar-revenue essential-services enterprises (HVAC, plumbing, roofing, pet care, wellness, hospitality, automotive) and their end customers, handling inbound, outbound, analytics and dispatch so the operator supplies only the physical labor. She says over 70% of Netic customers are now 'Netic-first' — the AI handles the customer's first interaction — and that Netic has generated over $600M for customers from AI-handled interactions. She argues vertical software beats AI roll-ups on product leverage, dismisses the frontier labs as a competitive risk in essential services, places robotics for the trades decades out, and says private equity's playbook has shifted from buying undiscovered gems to creating tangible value while still opening every conversation on cost cutting rather than net-new revenue.

themes.theme: Netic's wedge between service enterprises and end customers

insights.claim: Netic sells AI agents to large essential-services enterprises — HVAC, plumbing, electrical, roofing, consumer wellness memberships, hospitality, automotive and pet services — positioning itself as the layer between the company and its millions of end customers that handles need discovery, matching against the business's operational rules, and deployment of labor.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: Defines a vertical-AI category monetizing the customer-interaction layer of fragmented, PE-heavy service industries rather than the labor itself — a different exposure than robotics or roll-up bets.
insights.quote: So netic exists between the company and its customers.

insights.claim: Netic's target buyer is a roughly billion-dollar-revenue home or consumer services company, frequently private-equity owned and run as an EBITDA business, whose growth is structurally capped because any expansion requires continuously hiring more back-office people.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: Names the exact economic constraint — headcount-linked growth inside margin-sensitive EBITDA assets — that makes agentic software an easy ROI sell into PE-owned service platforms.

insights.claim: Routing in essential services is far more complex than call answering: the agent must establish what equipment is in the home, whether the company can service it at all, same-day versus next-day urgency, the customer's lifetime value, and whether to send the technician qualified for boilers versus newer systems.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: The operational-complexity layer is where vertical AI defends against generic voice-agent vendors — diligence competitors on whether they model technician skill and lifetime value, not just pickup rate.

insights.claim: Essential services are commoditized at the point of demand, so an unanswered inquiry is instantly lost to the next result — and customers now find providers through aggregators, search engines and increasingly LLMs.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: Makes answer-rate a direct revenue-capture metric, and flags LLM chat as an emerging local-services lead channel alongside Google search.
insights.quote: If you do not answer me, I'm going to go to the next one, next search result on Google, next result on like now charg.

insights.claim: Netic has moved beyond overflow call handling: over 70% of its customers are now 'Netic-first' (internally 'N1'), meaning the end customer's first interaction with the business is with a Netic agent rather than a human.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: The shift from overflow to primary channel is the key adoption milestone for voice-agent companies — it signals pricing power and durable displacement of in-house and outsourced call centers.
insights.quote: But today actually over 70% of our customers are AI first. We call it netic first. They go N1.

insights.claim: Netic claims it has generated over $600 million of revenue for its customers from AI-handled interactions, and sells against live deployments rather than demos.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: A cumulative customer-revenue-generated figure is the benchmark to hold other agent vendors to, and implies Netic can price on value or revenue share rather than seats.
insights.quote: we have made so far, I think over $600 million for our customers that have been really generated from AI handled interactions

themes.theme: Vertical AI software vs. AI roll-ups

insights.claim: Melissa Tokmak rejected the AI roll-up path — buying and optimizing service businesses, as Long Lake does — on three grounds: what she wanted to build in the world, skill-set fit (roll-ups are M&A-led and she is an engineer and product person), and the achievable scale of the product.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: A usable screen for service-industry AI founders: back operators on roll-ups and product-led founders on software, because the core competency of a roll-up is deal-making.
insights.quote: I'm a builder. I am an engineer. I'm a product person.

insights.claim: The structural ceiling on tech-enabled roll-ups is that every product built applies only to the companies already acquired and cannot be sold to any other operator, capping product leverage versus a platform serving all operators in the vertical.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: Argues roll-up software value accrues as asset-level EBITDA instead of compounding software multiples — a direct valuation argument between two models chasing the same customers.
insights.quote: but at the end all the products you're building are for the company you just bought. it can't really be actually applied to any other company.

insights.claim: Netic's stated endgame is the 'autonomous enterprise': every function inside these companies handled autonomously except the physical service and labor, with each product built on a shared intelligence layer that compounds and connects to the others.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: If achievable, the software layer captures an industry's entire coordination margin while operators become labor-supply businesses — a repricing of where value sits in services.
insights.quote: We are building an autonomous enterprise,

themes.theme: Why the frontier labs aren't the competitive risk here

insights.claim: Enterprises in essential services are structurally poor customers for lab-built products because the labs ship fast and kill products fast, which conflicts with the multi-year reliability mission-critical buyers require.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: Product-deprecation risk is an underrated moat for vertical vendors; lab sunset announcements are a churn catalyst pushing enterprises toward specialists.
insights.quote: open AI builds amazing products really fast but also it kills them

insights.claim: Focus explains why Anthropic pulled ahead in coding agents, but the labs show the opposite pattern in enterprise, where roughly 20 overlapping products make their strategy unreadable — so the startups genuinely at risk are those whose products look functionally and visually like a lab's core surface, a chatbot or a coding agent.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete lab-risk filter — proximity to the labs' shipped surface area — and suggests unfocused lab enterprise efforts leave a durable window for vertical incumbents.

insights.claim: Lab researchers optimize for the most generalizable solution, so their implicit answer to a vertical problem is 'when we get AGI we'll ask it how to solve essential services' — which Melissa Tokmak calls both operationally and intellectually lazy.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: The generalization incentive inside labs is the structural reason vertical last-mile value persists — a direct counter to the view that application-layer companies are transient.
insights.quote: well when we get the a AGI we'll ask how to solve it for essential services and I think that is both operationally and intellectually a bit lazy thinking

insights.claim: Serving millions of end customers with different worries, accents and contexts — and re-engaging them into repeat business — requires last-mile work that models alone don't provide, so vertical AI companies must be good at all three layers: models, harnesses and orchestration, and the software product on top.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: A three-layer competence test for diligencing agent companies — model wrappers lack the orchestration and product layers where retention actually lives.
insights.quote: So if anything actually companies like us and Netic have to be good at all three layers.

insights.claim: Unlike the 2021-22 cohort the host funded (Harvey, Perplexity, later Decagon and Abridge), founders today are so worried about lab roadmaps that they avoid entering verticals they think a lab might touch — which Melissa Tokmak attributes to company building optimized for an immediate exit.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil (host)
insights.so_what: If founder self-deterrence is real, whitespace verticals are currently under-supplied with startups — a sourcing edge for investors willing to fund perceived lab adjacency.
insights.quote: there's a lot of building going on currently that's focused on how can I exit immediately

themes.theme: Robotics timeline for the physical trades

insights.claim: Melissa Tokmak places robotics for home-services trades decades out, arguing that for robots to do what Netic's customers do today every building would have to be 3D printed or fully standardized, which she does not expect to happen.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: A bearish near-term read on automating physical labor in the built environment — the investable near-term layer is coordination software, not humanoids.
insights.quote: If robotics is going to do what we're doing with these companies today, every single of those buildings need to be either 3D printed

insights.claim: The specific robotics blockers in home services are dexterity across varied screw and fixture types, navigating tiny spaces and non-standard home layouts, and diagnostic ambiguity where walls must be opened before the problem is even visible — plus a human element because customers often engage on the worst day of their lives.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: Provides concrete capability milestones — dexterity plus in-situ diagnosis — to watch before repricing service-labor businesses for automation risk.

insights.claim: The private equity playbook has already changed: finding an undiscovered gem at an attractive multiple, swapping the team and reselling no longer works because those gems don't exist anymore, forcing sponsors toward creating tangible operating value inside the businesses they own.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: Value creation replacing multiple arbitrage makes PE portfolios a structurally motivated buyer pool for operational AI — the core demand driver for vendors selling into sponsors.
insights.quote: But those gems don't really exist anymore like undiscovered.

insights.claim: Some sponsors over-lean into AI by evaluating agents like deterministic software — judging a platform on its first week instead of treating deployment as the start of a relationship whose results must hold and improve across the year — while others are institutionalizing capability by hiring AI operating partners and AI-forward engineers who then educate portfolio companies.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: Mis-specified one-week pilots produce false negatives on agent vendors; AI operating partners are the new buying center and the channel for portfolio-wide standardization.

insights.claim: First conversations with private equity owners still default to cost cutting, and Netic has to actively reframe the pitch toward net-new revenue with tangible live examples because sponsors otherwise anchor on the bottom line.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: Revenue-generating AI is currently under-priced by sponsors relative to cost-out AI, which is a positioning edge for any vendor that can prove top-line lift.
insights.quote: I'm not really there to cut your costs.

insights.claim: A private equity owner holding 20-30 businesses across different verticals could use a shared customer-context layer to cross-sell between them — steering a dog owner toward the wellness membership that also offers pet care.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: Cross-portfolio customer context is the sponsor-level prize a single-operator roll-up can't replicate — the strongest argument for standardizing an entire portfolio on one AI platform.

themes.theme: Selling AI into supposedly 'old school' service industries

insights.claim: It is a misconception that essential-services operators are slow technology adopters — Melissa Tokmak says some of the most tech-forward owners she has met run these businesses, which she characterizes as extremely primal and tech-forward at the same time.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: Undercuts the standard bear case on adoption speed in the trades — sales-cycle assumptions for these verticals may be far too conservative.
insights.quote: I think the way that I think about these industries is that they are extremely primal and tech forward at the same time.

insights.claim: Netic closed a roughly half-million-dollar contract end to end in 14 days, which Melissa Tokmak attributes to these buyers being rigorously value-focused rather than credulous about AI.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: A concrete velocity benchmark — mid-six-figure contract value in two weeks — far faster than typical enterprise software cycles, supporting capital-efficient go-to-market in this category.
insights.quote: just one of the businesses we closed it can be like a half a million contract um and it took from end to end 14 days

insights.claim: For roofing customers Netic feeds satellite data on how hurricanes affected specific neighborhoods and which materials to use directly into its agents' context, so one platform both improves inbound conversations and identifies which homes to target with outbound and door knockers — replacing the separate tools and manual analysis operators used before.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: Shows the expansion path from call handling into demand generation where proprietary external data becomes the moat — a far larger revenue opportunity per customer than contact-center replacement.

themes.theme: Hiring for agency and long-horizon company building

insights.claim: Melissa Tokmak says Gen Z candidates increasingly operate under a 'permanent underclass mentality' — that failing to make money within 18 months or learn everything within six months means being poor forever — which she links to an AGI-pilled belief that AI will subsume human skill sets and calls a dangerous mindset because building good things takes a very long time.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: A labor-market read on how AGI expectations compress time horizons, predicting shorter tenures and higher churn across AI startups.
insights.quote: I see especially Gen Z in these days when I'm you know looking at hiring obsessed with this permanent underclass mentality

insights.claim: Netic screens for demonstrated agency plus follow-through — asking what the hardest thing a candidate has ever done was, in or outside work, then digging in on whether they sustained it rather than doing it for a weekend — explicitly avoids shiny-object seekers, and requires every engineer to visit customer sites before building product back in San Francisco.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: A transferable rubric for AI-era teams where persistence and field grounding, not tool familiarity, are the scarce inputs to correct product decisions.
insights.quote: every single engineer in our company do have to go visit customers on site to build the right product back home in San Francisco

insights.claim: Melissa Tokmak frames craftsmanship over signaling with a quote attributed to Martin Luther — the Christian shoemaker honors God by making the best shoe, not by putting crosses on it — and names sustaining a remarkable-people-only bar as her second northstar after the autonomous-enterprise vision, noting Palantir, SpaceX and Notion all struggled with it while scaling.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: Talent-density decay is the recognized failure mode of scaling AI companies; hiring-bar discipline and product craft over AI branding are leading indicators worth tracking in diligence.
insights.quote: it says you know the Christian shoe maker, you know, doesn't honor God by putting little crosses on the shoes.

themes.theme: Access, agency and the AI narrative

insights.claim: Melissa Tokmak's top non-Netic AI excitement is education, grounded in going from a small Turkish town where she didn't own a computer — messaging high-school alumni on Facebook Messenger for essay feedback — to a full Stanford scholarship; she argues AI removes resourcing and access as the binding constraints.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: Points to education as the consumer AI category she expects the most surplus from, and frames access rather than capability as the variable now being solved.

insights.claim: Melissa Tokmak pushes back on 'you can just go do things' optimism: removing resource constraints doesn't change that the majority of the world still won't make the choice to act, so cheaper access has a dystopian side — and she expects mainstream US AI discourse, currently very negative, to shift as first-touch use cases become help-in-crisis moments, education and understanding your own health records.
insights.speaker: Melissa Tokmak
insights.so_what: Tempers total-addressable-market math built on 'AI democratizes X' — adoption may be motivation-gated rather than access-gated — and flags help-oriented verticals as where a sentiment turn shows up first.
insights.quote: It would be pretty sad if we used AI only for cost cutting.
